newsitem.title: INDIA: Top Indian official slams domestic industry lobby.
newsitem.headline: Top Indian official slams domestic industry lobby.

text.p: The highest-ranking civil servant in India's Industry Ministry criticised government colleagues for blocking foreign investment in the aviation and media industries, the Economic Times said on Tuesday.

In an interview to the newspaper, Industry Secretary Nilmadhab Mohanty said "malignant lobbying" by domestic players had delayed an attempt to clear a $600 million venture between Singapore Airlines and India's Tata group.
"The lobbying that has gone into deferring the Tata-SIA (Singapore International Airlines) venture is an example of malignant lobbying," Mohanty was quoted as saying.

"The lobbyists conveniently used the pretext that (state-run) Indian Airlines would be affected. But actually, they were acting on behalf of certain private airlines that did not want quality competition to be introduced in the domestic aviation sector."
Last week, India allowed foreign investors to hold stakes of up to 40 percent in domestic airlines, but held back approval for direct equity holding by foreign airlines.
Mohanty's words flew in the face of Civil Aviation Minister C.M. Ibrahim, who has publicly opposed the Singapore Airlines venture.

"Will Singapore or Indonesia allow any of our airlines in their domestic sector? I as an Indian should not allow foreign airlines in our domestic sector," Ibrahim was quoted on Tuesday by the Times of India newspaper as saying.

Without naming anyone, Mohanty signalled there was opposition within the government to some aspects of liberalisation of foreign investment that India undertook when it launched an economic reforms programme in 1991.
"When we are committed to something, and if there is a delay, it can be frustrating," Mohanty was quoted as saying. He said the government should allow foreign media to broadcast from Indian soil.
"The foreign media has already come into India," he said, referring to cable television broadcasters beaming programmes to India from abroad after making the programmes in the country.

"Today, without uplinking, these channels are taking signals out of the country and sending it back into the country and throughout the world. There is no monitoring of the content. Now, if uplinking is allowed in India, a certain amount of scrutiny can actually be introduced," Mohanty said.

India decided on Monday to set up a cabinet sub-committee to consider uplinking, or broadcasting from Indian soil, by private broadcasters to end a decades-old state monopoly over the airwaves with the help of a new broadcast law.
Mohanty said he also favoured the government giving up its majority in state-owned companies to improve their efficiency.
"In the Indian context, the only way out is to bring down the government's stake to below 50 percent," he said.
Mohanty is scheduled to retire this week and take up a United Nations assignment.
